title: Foundations of Software Architecture
description: What architecture is, the two values of software, and what good architecture enables.

children.title: Design, Architecture, and the Two Values
children.description: Design vs architecture and the behaviour/structure value tension.
source_sections: Design, Architecture, and the Two Values

learning_objectives.text: Explain why the distinction between design and architecture is artificial — both form a continuous fabric of decisions.
Compare the two values of software (behaviour and structure) and justify why structure is the greater value over time.
Identify the symptoms of a system whose architecture has been neglected in favour of feature delivery.

children.title: What Good Architecture Enables
children.description: Facilitating development, deployment, operation, and maintenance while keeping options open.

learning_objectives.text: List the four activities good architecture must facilitate: development, deployment, operation, and maintenance.
Explain why 'keeping options open' — deferring decisions about details — is the core strategy of good architecture.
Describe how team size changes the architectural pressure on a codebase.
By the end of this topic, you will be able to explain what software architecture is and why structure is as valuable as behaviour.

title: Design Principles
description: SOLID and the component principles, condensed.

children.title: The SOLID Principles
children.description: All five SOLID principles with their violation symptoms and remedies.
source_sections: The SOLID Principles at a Glance

learning_objectives.text: State all five SOLID principles and the design problem each addresses.
Diagnose which SOLID principle a described design violates and propose the standard remedy.

children.title: Component Principles
children.description: Component cohesion (REP, CCP, CRP) and coupling (ADP, SDP, SAP) in brief.

learning_objectives.text: Explain the tension between the three component-cohesion principles.
Detect and break a component dependency cycle.
By the end of this topic, you will be able to apply SOLID and component principles when organizing classes, modules, and components.

title: Clean Architecture
description: The Dependency Rule, boundaries, and keeping details (database, web, frameworks) at arm's length.

children.title: Drawing Boundary Lines
children.description: Business rules vs details, and the plugin architecture idea.

learning_objectives.text: Explain why the database and the GUI are plugins to the business rules, not the other way around.
Apply the plugin-architecture idea to position a new subsystem on the right side of a boundary.

children.title: The Dependency Rule and the Four Layers
children.description: Entities, use cases, interface adapters, frameworks & drivers — dependencies point inward.
source_sections: The Dependency Rule and the Four Layers

learning_objectives.text: Name the four layers of the Clean Architecture and what belongs in each.
Apply the Dependency Rule to decide whether a proposed dependency between two classes is legal.
Explain why the layer count is not fixed at four as long as the Dependency Rule holds.

children.title: Details: Database, Web, and Frameworks
children.description: Why the database, web, and frameworks are deferrable details.

learning_objectives.text: Argue why the database schema and the web delivery mechanism are details, not the architecture.
Describe the asymmetric-marriage risk of frameworks and strategies to use them while limiting coupling.
Identify the framework marriages that are practically unavoidable and how to contain them.
By the end of this topic, you will be able to design a system around the Dependency Rule with business rules independent of frameworks, UI, and databases.

title: Architecture Styles in Practice
description: Monoliths and layers, plus the step beyond: queues and events.

children.title: Monoliths and Layered Applications
children.description: All-in-one apps, layering, and traditional N-layer designs.

learning_objectives.text: Define a monolithic application and describe when single-project, all-in-one apps are appropriate.
Explain the benefits and costs of logical layering (UI, business logic, data access) inside a single deployment unit.
Analyze the dependency problem of traditional N-layer designs where business logic depends on data access.

children.title: Beyond the Monolith: Queues and Events
children.description: Web-Queue-Worker and event-driven architecture in brief.

learning_objectives.text: Describe the Web-Queue-Worker style and when it beats both monolith and microservices.
Differentiate pub/sub from event streaming and identify event-driven fits.
By the end of this topic, you will be able to select and justify an architecture style for a typical web workload.

title: Web Application Architecture
description: Front-end choice and the core server-side patterns of a modern web app.

children.title: Traditional Web Apps vs SPAs
children.description: Choosing server-rendered, SPA, or hybrid front ends.

learning_objectives.text: State the conditions favouring traditional web apps (simple client requirements, no-JS support, SEO) vs SPAs (rich UX, exposed API).
Use the decision table to recommend traditional, SPA, or Blazor for a described product.
Explain the staffing and tooling costs a SPA adds to a project.

children.title: Server-Side Patterns Essentials
children.description: MVC/Razor Pages, dependency injection, structure, security, and data access in brief.

learning_objectives.text: Outline how a server-side web app maps requests to responses through routing, model binding, and filters.
Apply dependency injection and feature organization to keep a web app testable.
Choose between a full ORM, a micro-ORM, and a NoSQL store for a workload.
By the end of this topic, you will be able to architect a maintainable, testable web application from the front end through data access.

title: API Design and Integration
description: REST design essentials and versioning an evolving API.

children.title: RESTful API Design Essentials
children.description: Resources, URIs, method semantics, pagination, HATEOAS, and OpenAPI in brief.

learning_objectives.text: Design resource URIs and choose correct HTTP methods and status codes.
Explain pagination, partial responses, HATEOAS, and OpenAPI's role in an API contract.

children.title: API Versioning
children.description: URI, query-string, header, and media-type versioning trade-offs.

learning_objectives.text: Compare the four explicit versioning mechanisms and their effects on caching and client code.
Choose a versioning strategy for a public API and justify it against breaking-change policy.
By the end of this topic, you will be able to design and implement a well-behaved, versioned, documented web API.

title: Scalability and Distributed Systems
description: CAP and consistency, availability math, database scaling, caching, and queues.

children.title: Performance, Scalability, and CAP
children.description: Performance vs scalability, latency vs throughput, CAP, and consistency patterns.

learning_objectives.text: Distinguish a performance problem from a scalability problem and latency from throughput.
Apply the CAP theorem to classify a data store as CP or AP for a given failure scenario.
Match weak, eventual, and strong consistency models to appropriate use cases.

children.title: Availability Patterns
children.description: Fail-over modes and availability arithmetic.

learning_objectives.text: Compare active-passive and active-active fail-over including their data-loss risks.
Calculate composite availability for components in sequence and in parallel.
Translate 99.9% and 99.99% availability into acceptable downtime per year.

children.title: Database Scaling
children.description: Replication, federation, sharding, denormalization, and SQL tuning.

learning_objectives.text: Select and combine replication, sharding, and partitioning strategies for a growing dataset.

children.title: Caching Essentials
children.description: Cache layers and update patterns.

children.title: Message and Task Queues
children.description: Queues, task queues, and back pressure.

learning_objectives.text: Explain how message queues decouple producers from consumers and smooth bursty load.
Apply back pressure when queue depth signals that the system is saturated.
By the end of this topic, you will be able to scale a web system by combining edge infrastructure, database scaling, caching, and asynchronous work.

title: Microservices
description: The essentials of microservice design — and a critical counterweight.

children.title: Microservices Essentials
children.description: What microservices are, when they pay off, and how services should communicate and own data.

learning_objectives.text: Describe the defining properties of microservices and their cost.
Choose communication patterns and data ownership rules for a small service system.

children.title: A Critical View of Services
children.description: Services alone are not an architecture: the decoupling and independence hypes examined.

learning_objectives.text: Explain why splitting into services does not by itself create architectural boundaries.
Critique the claims of total decoupling and independent development used to justify microservices.
Analyze the cross-cutting-change weakness of services decomposed purely by function, and the vertical-layers remedy.
By the end of this topic, you will be able to decompose a domain into microservices and design their communication, APIs, and data ownership.

title: Cloud-Native Operations
description: Twelve-factor discipline, safe deployments, retries, and observability in brief.

children.title: The Twelve Factors at a Glance
children.description: All twelve factors condensed to their operational core.

learning_objectives.text: List the twelve factors and the failure each prevents.
Audit an app for the most commonly violated factors: config, statelessness, logs, and parity.

children.title: Deploy, Retry, Observe
children.description: Deployment strategies, transient-fault retries, and monitoring essentials.

learning_objectives.text: Compare rolling, blue-green, and canary deployments.
Design a retry policy with backoff and a circuit-breaking fallback.
By the end of this topic, you will be able to take a web system from commit to production with safe deployments, fault tolerance, and full observability.
